item.title: China's first carrier-borne armed reconnaissance stealth drone GJ-21 completes takeoff, landing aboard Type 076 amphibious assault ship
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 17:10:00
China's first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, the Sichuan, is underway on Nov. 15, 2025. The Sichuan returned to the shipyard in Shanghai at around 5 p.m. Sunday after completing its maiden sea trial. (Photo by Zhang Liang/Xinhua) China’s GJ-21 reconnaissance and strike stealth drone recently completed its first successful takeoff and landing aboard the Sichuan, the country’s first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, marking a breakthrough in the Chinese Navy’s ability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime combat platforms, according to the Xinhua News Agency. The GJ-21 is the Chinese military’s first carrier-borne stealth drone integrating reconnaissance and strike capabilities. Its successful takeoff and landing demonstrate the Chinese Navy’s capability to launch and recover fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime combat platforms. The airborne unmanned warfare formation attends a military parade in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 3, 2025. China on Wednesday held a grand gathering to commemorate the 80th anniversary of the victory in the Chinese People's War of Resistance against Japanese Aggression and the World Anti-Fascist War. (Xinhua/Deng Hua) The Sichuan, bearing hull number 51, is the first Type 076 amphibious assault ship independently designed, developed and built by China. Launched and named on December 27, 2024, it incorporates a fully automated landing guidance system, a new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult and arresting technology. It can carry fixed-wing drones, helicopters and amphibious equipment, according to Xinhua. Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan has steadily conducted sea trials as scheduled, successfully completing equipment and system checks and tests of overall operational stability, per Xinhua. item.title: Merz's flattery of Takaichi was politically frivolous
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 11:12:00
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi (R) and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hold a joint press conference after their talks at the prime minister's office in Tokyo on October 28, 2026. Photo: VCG During his visit to Japan, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stated that despite the geographical distance between the two countries, calling each other neighbors would not be an overstatement. He also described Germany and Japan as "Premium Partners," emphasizing that the two sides share similar interests and values. While expressing a sense of closeness is not unusual in diplomatic settings, characterizing two countries separated by 9,000 kilometers as "neighbors" - and using "shared values" as a pretext to advance a series of security and economic arrangements with clear, targeted objectives - goes well beyond mere rhetoric. By framing Germany and Japan as "neighbors," Merz is not truly referring to geography, but rather to political alignment. As developed economies, Germany and Japan share common interests in upholding multilateral trade and addressing climate change. However, these interests can be addressed through established bilateral and multilateral channels, without drawing lines based on "shared values." It is worth noting that Germany's postwar reflection on its own history has left a deep impression on nations across Asia. In contrast, since the current Japanese administration took office, there have been clear signs of a distorted view of history and moves toward "remilitarization," prompting neighboring countries to remain vigilant. By emphasizing "shared values" with Japan at this particular moment, how does Merz expect Asian countries to view Germany? In fact, Merz is doing more than just signaling closer ties with Japan; he has explicitly called for stronger military cooperation between the two countries. Germany has also expressed interest in joining the Global Combat Air Program - a joint initiative involving Japan, the UK, and Italy. The fact that two nations defeated in World War II are so eagerly moving to the forefront of military cooperation, while selectively emphasizing "shared values" and deliberately sidestepping the postwar international order's constraints on military activities, is in itself enough to warrant vigilance from the international community. On the Taiwan question, Merz also remarked that Germany will decide how to implement the one-China policy, an attempt to create a "gray area" on a matter of principle. Such attempts to test the boundaries are in no way constructive for China-Germany relations. Merz's flattery toward Takaichi goes beyond mere "cozying up" - it is a clear display of political frivolity. China has never opposed other nations developing normal relations; however, any cooperation implicitly directed against China deviates from the proper course of state-to-state relations. The German business community had generally hoped that Merz's trip to Asia would help secure orders and improve supply-chain links. Yet Merz has clearly failed to demonstrate the rationality expected of a mature political figure during this visit. The Chinese foreign ministry has previously expressed the hope that Germany and the EU will remain objective and rational, work with China in the same direction, and become reliable and predictable partners for each other. Merz would do well to heed this advice. One might attempt to "claim" a neighbor from 9,000 kilometers away, but genuine partnership requires sincerity and mutual respect.

item.title: From anxiety to calm: Chinese support transforms maternal, child healthcare in western Pakistan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 08:49:00
This file photo shows medical supplies donated by China at a hospital in Quetta, Pakistan. (Xinhua) For 28-year-old Gul Bano, the birth of her fourth child brought something she had not experienced during her previous three deliveries -- a sense of calm. Two months ago, Bano arrived at a basic health unit in the provincial capital city of Balochistan to give birth. Unlike her earlier experiences, she found herself surrounded by modern medical equipment, trained health workers, and a clean, well-equipped delivery room. "This time, I was not afraid," Bano said, recalling the day her baby was born. "Everything was available here, and the delivery was much easier than it was a few years ago." Among the equipment that assisted her was a vein detector, which makes it easier to locate veins, particularly when an intravenous line or blood sample is needed, as well as a vacuum extractor, making it easier for her to deliver. For Bano, however, the difference was not only about medical equipment. She said the care she received made her feel respected and comfortable. "My husband works as a daily-wage laborer and earns less than 5 U.S. dollars a day, hindering us as a family from affording quality healthcare. Here, everything was provided to me free of charge, even the delivery gown. The bed was clean, and the equipment was ready," she said. "I did not have to worry about anything." Her experience reflects the changes taking place in maternal and child healthcare facilities across Balochistan. Supported by the government of China, these facilities are offering safer and more dignified childbirth services for mothers. China has been helping the government of Balochistan in upgrading maternal and child healthcare facilities, including the improvement of 100 medical facilities across the province. The cooperation aims to strengthen medical infrastructure, provide modern equipment, and improve services for mothers and newborns, particularly in areas where access to quality healthcare has traditionally been difficult. For women like Bano, these improvements are not simply about new machines or renovated rooms, but can mean the difference between approaching childbirth with anxiety and facing it with confidence. "I am very happy with the treatment I received," she said. "I thank China for helping us. My fourth child arrived not only as a new member of the family, but also as a reminder of how better healthcare can change a mother's experience at one of the most important moments of her life." Balochistan has the highest maternal and neonatal mortality rates in Pakistan, largely because 70 percent of the population lives in remote, scattered and hard-to-reach areas, Sana Furqan, a medical practitioner at the Basic Health Unit in the Hudda locality of Quetta, told Xinhua. "For decades, access has been the biggest barrier. This China-supported project is the first large-scale targeted intervention focused entirely on mothers and children at the primary healthcare level, bringing life-saving care to the doorstep of women in remote districts," she said. Talking about the newly equipped healthcare facilities and renovation, Furqan said the Chinese government has supplied equipment like ultrasound machines, delivery beds, baby warmers, incubators, and essential laboratory equipment. "This upgrade is going to bring proximity, preparedness, timeliness and continuity, which is critical to prevent deaths from postpartum hemorrhage, sepsis and birth asphyxia," she said, adding that it will also provide solar solutions, ambulances, as well as training for female staff. "The project would have transformative impacts on the basic healthcare system of Balochistan. In the medium term, we expect a measurable reduction in maternal mortality ratio and neonatal mortality rate, and a sharp decline in preventable complications," she added. Furqan believes the assistance is not seen as charity, but as brotherhood. "The people of Balochistan, especially its mothers, will never forget that when they needed help the most, China stood with them." In a conversation with Xinhua, Provincial Health Minister Bakht Muhammad Kakar said that Pakistan-China cooperation in the health sector is opening a new chapter in people-centered development, turning the friendship between the two countries into tangible benefits for communities. China has one of the most advanced, efficient, and equitable healthcare systems in the world, Kakar said, underlining that despite its own vast population, the country has achieved universal maternal and child health coverage, which is an inspiration for Pakistan. "We want to learn from China's experience in maternal health monitoring, village doctor system, and digital health records," the health minister said.

item.title: Thai medical student finds a calling in acupuncture
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 08:46:00
Salocha Techawanwanitchakorn (R) performs acupuncture on a patient under the guidance of her mentor at the First Teaching Hospital of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in Tianjin, north China, Sept. 10, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Runzhi) A Thai intern gently slid a fine silver needle into an acupoint on a hemiplegic patient's leg. She lifted, thrust and twirled it -- and the motionless leg twitched. Salocha Techawanwanitchakorn, an intern at the First Teaching Hospital of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) in north China, had just felt what she came to China to learn. "At that moment," she said, "I knew I had made the right choice to study TCM." Techawanwanitchakorn grew up around the herbal shops of Bangkok's Chinatown, where the air was thick with the scent of Chinese medicine. Her Chinese grandmother was a regular there, buying herbs, and the family relied on TCM to stay healthy. As a child, Techawanwanitchakorn saw TCM as little more than bitter brews and needles. She didn't understand it, but a seed had already been planted. Later, Techawanwanitchakorn came to Tianjin for high school. A class visit to the First Teaching Hospital of Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine gave her a first close look at TCM. "I was struck," she said. "TCM doesn't just ease symptoms. It treats the root cause." That visit convinced her to study TCM there, and later she entered Tianjin University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. Getting to grips with TCM was not easy. In her first year, concepts like meridians and "qi," or vital energy -- invisible and intangible -- left Techawanwanitchakorn baffled. Classical texts full of traditional characters read like a book from another world. None of it deterred the Thai student, however. The following year, Techawanwanitchakorn began studying acupuncture, practicing on herself first. "I felt soreness, numbness, distension and an electric-like tingle at acupoints on my own limbs," she said. "Only then did I know how to put a patient at ease." "Even if a patient's symptoms improve by half, I'm happy," said Techawanwanitchakorn, who specializes in acupuncture as a graduate student. During her clinical internship, Techawanwanitchakorn kept a notebook in her white coat pocket, filled with Chinese and Thai notes on acupoints, prescriptions and the key points her teachers stressed. She came to understand that needling is not just about finding the right acupoint, but about feeling the needle sensation under her hand. Since patients differ in build, the angle and depth of insertion must be adjusted accordingly. The longer she studied under her Chinese teachers, the more she realized that hands-on skill was only the first step. "A good doctor sees not only the disease but also the person," her mentor told her. At first, patients took her accent as a sign that she was from southern China. When they learned she was Thai, some greeted her with "Sawasdee kha (hello)," and said "Khob khun kha (thank you)" after she removed the needles. Others said she was the best foreign student at needling they had ever seen. "Experience is built needle by needle," Techawanwanitchakorn said. In clinical practice, Techawanwanitchakorn has seen more and more patients recover through acupuncture, and has come to appreciate TCM's unique strength in treating the whole patient. Her resolve to study TCM has only grown firmer. TCM, she believes, remains full of vitality after being passed down for thousands of years. In Thailand, too, many hospitals have TCM departments, and more young Thais are willing to try it. Techawanwanitchakorn, being one of them, has brought TCM home. Last summer, back in Thailand, she administered acupuncture to her sister, who had back pain. Though afraid of needles at first, her sister later said she felt "much more relaxed." Techawanwanitchakorn also used cupping equipment brought from China to treat her mother. In her daily life, she has adopted TCM-inspired habits, drinking chrysanthemum tea and paying more attention to her routine. The student is now interning while preparing for China's physician licensing exam. She hopes to stay in China first to gain clinical experience, then return to Thailand to promote TCM. "China has more patients and more complex cases, so there is more to learn," she said. "I will bring what I learned in China back to Thailand and let more people see the charm of TCM."

item.title: China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative named UN World Restoration Flagship
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-30 08:13:00
China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative is named a World Restoration Flagship by the United Nations during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, Oct. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Chen Junfeng) China's Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was named a World Restoration Flagship by the United Nations on Thursday during the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia. The initiative is jointly led by China's Ministry of Natural Resources and Ministry of Finance. This marks the second time a nationwide ecological restoration initiative from China has received the United Nations Decade on Ecosystem Restoration recognition, making China the first country to achieve the distinction twice. Chosen from over 200 applications and more than 80 government-submitted nominations, the Blue Bay Restoration Initiative was recognized as one of the world's most promising, ambitious and inspiring examples of large-scale ecosystem restoration, said Inger Andersen, executive director of the UN Environment Programme. The initiative aims to restore more than 150,000 hectares of coastal wetlands and over 2,000 km of coastline by 2030, bringing lasting benefits to local communities, she added.

item.title: To understand the new 'Made in China' era, the West must shed prejudices: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29 23:26:00
Dozens of UBTECH industrial humanoid robots carry out training tasks at a smart factory in the Qianwan New Area in Ningbo, East China's Zhejiang Province, on March 1, 2025. Photo: VCG The new face of "Made in China" is a transition from advantages of scale to systemic strengths, from cost competitiveness to innovation prowess, and from exporting goods to exporting capabilities. What the West truly needs to update is its entrenched mind-set of viewing China's development as a "zero-sum threat." On Thursday, Reuters published an article titled "Welcome to the new 'Made in China.'" Coining the term "new 'Made in China,'" the piece observed that Chinese manufacturing is expanding from cheap clothing, furniture, and toys into automobiles, complex machinery, high-end chemicals, and data center equipment. However, reading between the lines, the report remains accustomed to attributing China's competitiveness to subsidies, low prices, and "overcapacity." What does the new "Made in China" truly look like? Detaching oneself from an understanding of industrial ecosystems and competitive dynamics easily leads to the fallacy of "the blind men and the elephant" - mistaking a single leg for the entire creature. China's manufacturing sector is increasingly serving as the "factory of factories" supporting global industrial production. The strength of Chinese manufacturing is demonstrated not only in finished consumer products, but even more so in its capacity to provide critical equipment and foundational inputs for global production. Today, from precision control boards and specialized cabling to high-end machine tools and industrial robotics, Chinese manufacturing has become an indispensable component of global industrial upgrading and AI computing infrastructure. In the first three quarters of 2026, equipment manufacturing contributed nearly 90 percent of China's export growth. This vividly confirms a broader transition: China is steadily evolving from a provider of consumer goods into a pivotal supply-side hub for global productive capacity, while the bedrock of its competitiveness has upgraded from single-product price advantages to the systemic operational efficiency of an entire industrial ecosystem. The competitiveness of Chinese manufacturing has forged ahead through thorough market competition and continuous innovation. While subsidies may influence short-term costs, they can never replace a firm's long-term accumulation built through the process of market trial and error, process refinement, and rapid responsiveness to demand. Supported by an ultra-large domestic market, full-chain industrial integration, and a vast pool of engineering talent, new technologies in China swiftly transition from laboratory concepts to mass production before diffusing into adjacent sectors. Manufacturing competition itself has escalated into a contest of cross-industry technology transfer: perception and localization technologies developed for new-energy vehicles are spilling over into smart equipment, while the consumer robotics sector has pivoted from price wars toward competition over quality and brand reputation. Overseas consumer perceptions of Chinese products are similarly shifting - from "low price" to "technologically advanced and reliable." Brand premiums are increasingly determined by the speed of innovation and user acclaim. Dismissing the growth of Chinese manufacturing simply with terms like "subsidies" and "dumping" is not only factually incorrect, but also misreads the trajectory of global industry. Chinese manufacturing is evolving from exporting individual products to delivering comprehensive solutions. Research and development, design, manufacturing, digital operations and maintenance, and after-sales services are becoming deeply integrated. Industrial equipment manufacturers now provide customers with remote monitoring, preventive maintenance, and full lifecycle management, while logistics equipment companies integrate forklifts, warehousing systems, and digital platforms to improve customers' overall production efficiency. What Chinese companies deliver is no longer just individual pieces of hardware, but also the operation of entire production lines and support for complete production systems. The focus of value creation is consequently shifting toward system integration and long-term services. Meanwhile, China continues to advance institutional opening-up, making it clear that goods manufactured in China that meet domestic product standards are eligible for relevant government procurement support policies on an equal basis, regardless of whether their producers are domestic or foreign-invested enterprises. This latest round of upgrading is also opening up broader opportunities for global companies to participate in the Chinese market and leverage China's comprehensive industrial ecosystem. Trade barriers cannot override the economic forces that underpin industrial competitiveness. Tariffs may alter trade routes, but they cannot conjure up mature supply chains, a well-established pool of engineering talent, or deeply integrated industrial capabilities. Erecting barriers against Chinese intermediate goods and production equipment would instead raise the overall costs of industrial investment and technological upgrading in the countries imposing them. For countries determined to revitalize domestic manufacturing, shutting out cost-effective production inputs would not only fail to deliver the intended benefits but could also undermine the competitiveness of their domestic companies in third-country markets. The new face of "Made in China" is a transition from advantages of scale to systemic strengths, from cost competitiveness to innovation prowess, and from exporting goods to exporting capabilities. Every country has the right to develop its manufacturing sector, and every country has opportunities to participate in the international division of labor and benefit from technological progress. What the West truly needs to update is its entrenched mind-set of viewing China's development as a "zero-sum threat." Only by approaching competition with an open mind can countries create room for cooperation, and only by respecting objective economic laws can they turn the global trend of industrial upgrading into tangible opportunities for mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.

item.title: GT Voice: SK shipbuilding's high-end edge hinges on Asian industrial collaboration
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-29 22:12:00
Visitors check out ship models at a booth during the Offshore Korea 2026 held in Busan, South Korea on October 14, 2026. Photo: VCG South Korea's shipbuilders posted third-quarter profits driven by high value vessels; however, sustaining their high end edge calls for regional industrial collaboration rather than yielding to external geopolitical demands that risk eroding long term industrial strengths. HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering announced on Wednesday that its third-quarter operating profit rose 37.3 percent year-on-year, driven by higher ship prices and strong earnings from its engine and offshore businesses, The Korea Herald reported. This strong performance is far from an isolated case. South Korea's three major shipbuilders all achieved relatively robust results in the third quarter of this year. Samsung Heavy Industries announced that its operating profit for the quarter increased by 42 percent year-on-year, bringing the combined operating profit of the three shipbuilders to 2.27 trillion won ($1.7 billion). This growth is attributed to continued revenue from high-value-added vessels, such as liquefied natural gas carriers. Behind these numbers lies the payoff of South Korea's shipbuilding sector in terms of high-value ship segments, a clear sign that it retains formidable competitiveness in premium shipbuilding markets. Yet the realization of the high-end ship dividend does not mean that competition will ease. High profitability tends to attract more resources into the high-end market. Global new ship orderbooks have seen China's share steadily rise amid intensifying market competition. If South Korea relies solely on the brand and technological reputation it has built up while neglecting supply-chain efficiency and sustained research and development, its high-end edge could be gradually squeezed. Holding the leading position requires more than winning high-priced orders; it demands stable delivery, consolidation of core supporting industries, cultivation of technical talent, and the continuous creation of new product advantages. This is precisely why South Korea's shipbuilding sector needs stable regional industrial collaboration more than ever. After decades of growth, Asia's shipbuilding industrial chain has formed a close, sophisticated division of labor that cannot be easily severed. The interconnected ecosystem spans parts supply, materials and equipment, vessel design technology, and specialized skilled personnel. Even as companies across the region compete fiercely for new orders, they can still identify shared interests in supply chain coordination, technical exchanges, and alignment of industry standards. To channel all their resources into technological upgrades and consolidate their hold on high-end segments, South Korea's shipbuilders need the support of the Asian industrial ecosystem. The coexistence of competition and cooperation has become a reality for Asia's shipbuilding landscape. Any attempt to break these deeply integrated industrial ties will ultimately undermine South Korea's own core competitiveness. At this critical juncture, persistent efforts by the US to poach South Korean shipbuilding capacity and pull it into its own industrial arrangements deserve particular vigilance. Such "cooperation" may appear to bring new orders and market access, but if its essence is to steer South Korean firms to channel their capital, technology, talent, and key production capacity toward serving America's industrial goals, South Korea must carefully assess the long-term costs. Shipbuilding is not a single factory that can be relocated at will. Its competitiveness is built on decades of accumulated supplier networks, engineering expertise, and seamless industrial collaboration. Restructuring production outside this established system will not only drive up costs across supply chains, personnel training, and operational coordination, but also divert resources that should be dedicated to South Korea's own industrial upgrading, potentially allowing its clearly laid-out development roadmap to be hijacked by external strategic priorities. Whether South Korea's shipbuilding sector can hold onto today's achievements will depend entirely on its willingness to keep innovating amid intensifying competition and seizing the initiative while deepening mutually beneficial regional cooperation. By expanding pragmatic regional collaboration, South Korea can turn its current profit into a solid foundation for long-term growth. Advancing regional cooperation is a key way for South Korea to translate today's profits into a foundation for lasting growth, rather than gradually consuming the industrial advantages in the course of catering to external geopolitical demands.
